question.text: What is the significance of the 'burden of proof' concept as it applies under PMLA?

answer.text: The burden lies on the accused to prove that the property is not involved in money laundering
The prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that money laundering occurred
The financial institution must prove it followed all KYC norms
The FIU-IND must prove the suspicious transaction report was accurate

explanation.text: The Logic: The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 operates under a reverse-burden framework. Under Section 24, once certain foundational facts about the proceeds of crime are established, the law presumes the property is involved in money laundering, and the onus shifts to the accused to prove that it is not. This is a departure from the ordinary criminal-law position where the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The Trap: A general criminal-law answer ("prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt") is wrong specifically for PMLA. The burden does not rest on the financial institution to prove KYC compliance, nor on FIU-IND to prove the accuracy of an STR — those are operational/regulatory obligations, not the statutory burden-of-proof rule. Note: The Section 24 reverse-burden / presumption provision is set out in the PMLA itself. It was not located in the cited NISM-Series-XXIV AML/CFT workbook pages (28-29, 88, 92); those pages support the section list, Section 5 attachment, recordkeeping, and proceeds-of-crime/STR context, but not the burden-of-proof rule. The framing above reflects the statute rather than a direct workbook citation.
